title: Merge K Sorted Lists
statement: You get k linked lists, each already sorted from small to large. Merge them all into one sorted linked list and return its head. Some lists may be empty, and k itself may be zero.

example.caption: Three sorted lists become one sorted list. Equal values (the two 1s, the two 4s) stay.

idea.sentence: The next value of the answer is always the smallest current head among the k lists, and a min-heap hands you that smallest head in log k time.

jargon.plain: A container where the smallest item is always on top. Adding or removing one item costs about log of its size.
The first node of a list that has not been used yet. It is the only node of that list that can be next.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a list of sorted arrays, e.g. [[1,4,5],[1,3,4],[2,6]]

vars.meaning: total number of nodes in all lists
number of lists (k in the problem)

compare.bruteLabel: Scan all m heads for the smallest each time

rows.name: Scan the heads each time
rows.note: For each of the n output nodes, look at up to m heads.

rows.name: Min-heap of heads
rows.note: The heap never holds more than one node per list. Each push or pop costs log m.

rows.name: Pairwise merge (divide and conquer)
rows.note: Merge lists two at a time, round after round. Not shown here. It reuses the merge-two-lists routine.

fast.takeaway: Only the k heads can be next, so the heap needs only k items. That is what turns a scan of m heads into a log m step.

stages.title: Heap of heads
stages.note: Push the head of every non-empty list into a min-heap. Skip null heads.

stages.title: Pop the smallest
stages.note: The top is the smallest unused value overall. Pop it and append it to the answer with a tail pointer.

stages.title: Push its successor
stages.note: The popped node's next node is now the head of that list. Push it, unless the list is used up.

stages.title: Return
stages.note: When the heap is empty every node has been placed. Return dummy.next.

edges.title: No lists at all
edges.why: The heap stays empty, the loop never runs, and dummy.next is null.

edges.title: Only empty lists
edges.why: Every head is null, so nothing is pushed. Pushing a null would crash on the first comparison.

edges.title: Equal values
edges.why: Ties are fine in a heap. Any of the equal nodes may come out first.

edges.title: Negative numbers
edges.why: Only comparisons are used, so the sign does not matter. Do not use 0 as a 'no value' marker for an empty list.

gotchas.text: Push a node's successor only after you pop it. Pushing all nodes up front works but makes the heap hold every node instead of k.
Filter out null heads before pushing. An empty list in the input is common.

There is no built-in heap. Do not fake one with array.sort() inside the loop, which costs O(m log m) per pop. If you ever sort numbers, remember the default sort compares as strings: [10, 9].sort() gives [10, 9].
With container/heap, call heap.Push(h, x) and heap.Pop(h). Calling h.Push or h.Pop directly only appends or removes the last slice item and does not restore the heap order.
Push and Pop on nodeHeap need a pointer receiver because they change the slice length. Len, Less and Swap can use a value receiver.

recap.key: Keep one head per list in a min-heap. Pop the smallest, append it, push its next node.
recap.complexity: Time O(n log m). Space O(m).
moves: Push each non-empty head into a min-heap
Pop the smallest and append it to the answer
Push the popped node's next, if any
Stop when the heap is empty. Return dummy.next
